overview.title: 📖 Overview: Measuring Time, Impurity, and Intoxication
overview.subtitle: Keritot 13a–13b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ אוֹכֵל אֲכִילָה אַחַת וְחַיָּיבִין עָלֶיהָ אַרְבָּעָה חַטָּאוֹת וְאָשָׁם אֶחָד
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the previous daf's open question about Rabbi Meir's time-window for eating a forbidden olive-bulk, confirming it as a stringency, and then tests Shmuel's parallel theory about impure foods against several baraitot — a test it fails. The Gemara works out exactly how food, liquid, and wine combine across multiple bites or sips to cross an impurity or Temple-entry threshold, including a puzzling ruling about a nursing infant whose mother contracted corpse-impurity. It then turns to the prohibition on a priest drinking wine before Temple service, parsing three different readings of 'wine and strong drink' that determine how much, and which beverages, actually disqualify him — with a real anecdote about Rav Ashi declining to rule after a festival meal. The daf closes with a striking new mishna: a single act of eating that generates liability for four separate sin offerings and one guilt offering simultaneously.

slides.title: 🕐 Settling the Time-Window Dispute
slides.subtitle: Confirming Rabbi Meir's standard, then testing — and refuting — Shmuel's parallel theory

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Gemara confirms: Rabbi Meir's 'as though eating roasted grain' standard is a stringency — liable even across a long stretch of time, so long as there's no gap between bites

2️⃣ Shmuel (via Ravnai) proposes a parallel rule for ritual impurity: eating a disqualifying quarter-loaf combines across an entire day, provided each individual olive-bulk was eaten within the shorter 'half-loaf' time-window
3️⃣ A baraita directly contradicts this: the entire quarter-loaf, start to finish, must fall within the half-loaf time-window to combine — not just each individual bite
4️⃣ The Gemara concludes bluntly: 'the refutation of Ravnai's view is a conclusive refutation' (תְּיוּבְתָּא)

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Both disputes hinge on the same underlying question: does a prohibition's minimum measure require continuous eating, or does each sub-measure only need its own brief window?

slides.title: 📏 Measuring Impurity Thresholds
slides.subtitle: A baraita's detailed rules for combining bites, sips, and Temple entry
rows: A quarter-loaf of impure food disqualifies eating teruma — but only if entirely consumed within the 'half-loaf' time-window, start to finish
A quarter-log of impure liquid works the same way — same time-window applies
One who ate less than the threshold may not immerse yet — doing so risks him wrongly believing a later completing bite needs no new immersion
May eat even large amounts of less-than-threshold impure food due to the danger of miscarriage
A quarter-log of wine, drunk within the half-loaf window, then entering and remaining in the Temple for that same duration, creates liability

callout.label: Common thread:
callout.text: Every one of these thresholds is measured not just by quantity, but by the pace at which it was consumed.

slides.title: 🍼 A Nursing Infant's Uncertain Status
slides.subtitle: If a mother contracted corpse-impurity, is the milk she nurses to her child impure?

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: The Sages permitted a woman impure through contact with a corpse to nurse her child, and the child remains pure.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But doesn't the child become impure by drinking impure milk, once that milk is rendered 'susceptible' by the wet drop on the nipple?

lines.speaker: Rava's first theory
lines.text: The place milk emerges from is like a 'spring' — inherently impure once the woman is, requiring no susceptibility at all (citing a mishna: milk transmits impurity even when not 'desired,' unlike ordinary liquids).

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But a baraita on the nine liquids of a zav treats milk like ordinary liquids (quarter-log threshold), not like saliva or urine (impure in any amount) — which a 'spring' status would require!

lines.speaker: Rava's real answer
lines.text: The true reason the child stays pure: it is doubtful whether he nursed the full threshold amount at all, and even if he did, doubtful whether it was within the required time-window — both uncertainties favor purity.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: A halakhic leniency built entirely on layered uncertainty (safek), not on any special exemption for nursing.

slides.title: 🍷 Wine and Temple Service — Three Readings of 'Wine and Strong Drink'
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 10:9 forbids a priest from drinking before entering the Tent of Meeting — but how much, and of what?

boxes.title: The first tanna
items: 'Strong drink' (שֵׁכָר) means specifically wine, learned by verbal analogy from the nazirite verse
Only a quarter-log of forty-day-old (fermented) wine triggers death at the hand of Heaven
Any lesser amount of wine is still forbidden by ordinary prohibition, just not the death penalty

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: 'Strong drink' includes any intoxicating beverage, not just wine
Wine specifically carries the death penalty; other intoxicants carry only an ordinary prohibition

boxes.title: Rabbi Elazar
items: 'Wine and strong drink' is one phrase, not two items — meaning wine consumed 'in its intoxicating manner'
Interrupting the drinking, or adding any water, exempts him entirely — the halakha follows this view

callout.label: Real-world footnote:
callout.text: Rav Ashi once postponed a ruling for Rav Aḥa of Huzal because he had just drunk wine at a festival meal — even diluted wine impairs judgment once more than a quarter-log was drunk.

slides.title: 🍽️ One Bite, Five Offerings
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's extreme case: a single act of eating triggers overlapping liability
rows: For eating notar (leftover consecrated meat past its time)
For eating consecrated food while ritually impure

callout.label: Rabbi Meir's rejected addition:
callout.text: He argued that if this bite also involved carrying the food from a private to a public domain on Shabbat, a sixth offering (for Shabbat desecration) should apply. The Rabbis disagreed: that liability stems from the act of carrying, not from the act of eating, so it does not belong on this list.

summary.principle: Every threshold of liability in these sugyot — how long one may take to eat, how much impure food or wine combines into a disqualifying measure, and how many distinct prohibitions a single bite can violate — is fixed by precise technical measures, never rough impression.

flowSteps.content: 🕐 Rabbi Meir's time-window is confirmed as a stringency; Shmuel's parallel theory for impurity is refuted by baraita
📏 Impurity thresholds (quarter-loaf, quarter-log) require the entire amount consumed within one continuous time-window
🍼 A nursing infant remains pure through layered uncertainty about quantity and timing, not through any special exemption

columns.content: 🍷 Three tannaitic readings define exactly how much of what beverage disqualifies a priest from Temple service
🍽️ A single bite can trigger four sin offerings and one guilt offering at once

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: halakhic liability is built from exact, stackable measures of quantity, time, and category — never a single blanket judgment

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's conclusion, is Rabbi Meir's 'roasted grain' time-window standard a stringency or a leniency?
o: A leniency, exempting anyone who interrupts their eating
A stringency — one remains liable even across a long period, as long as there is no interruption
Neither — it has no practical effect
A leniency that applies only on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes from the Rabbis' own phrasing ('unless he expends more than the time of eating a half-loaf') that Rabbi Meir's standard is a stringency: liable even over an extended period, so long as the eating is continuous.

quiz.q: What was the Gemara's verdict on Ravnai's theory that impure food combines across an entire day as long as each individual olive-bulk was eaten within the shorter half-loaf time-window?
o: It was accepted as the definitive halakha
It was refuted by a baraita requiring the ENTIRE quarter-loaf, start to finish, to fall within the half-loaf window
It applies only to liquids, not solids
It was left as an unresolved dispute
quiz.e: A baraita explicitly requires that from the start of the first bite to the end of the last bite, the total time must not exceed the half-loaf window — directly contradicting and refuting Ravnai's theory.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final explanation, why does a nursing infant remain pure even though his mother contracted corpse-impurity?
o: Because a mother's milk can never become impure
Because it is doubtful whether the infant nursed the disqualifying amount at all, and even if he did, doubtful whether it was within the required time-window
Because infants are always exempt from impurity laws
Because the milk was diluted with water
quiz.e: Rava concludes that the leniency rests on layered uncertainty — doubt about whether the infant consumed the threshold quantity, and further doubt about whether it happened within the necessary time-window — not on any inherent purity of the milk.

quiz.q: According to the halakha (following Rabbi Elazar), what happens if a priest drinks a quarter-log of wine but interrupts his drinking partway through, or adds any amount of water to it?
o: He is fully liable regardless
He is exempt from liability for entering the Temple afterward
He must wait an additional day before entering the Temple
He is liable only to lashes, not death
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar holds that the prohibition is drinking wine 'in the manner of intoxication'; interrupting the drinking or diluting it with any water exempts the priest, and the halakha follows this opinion.

quiz.q: In the mishna's extreme case of one act of eating generating multiple liabilities, which of the following combinations is described?
o: Four sin offerings and one guilt offering, for eating forbidden fat that was also notar, from consecrated food, while impure, on Yom Kippur
One sin offering and four guilt offerings
Five identical sin offerings for the same transgression
No liability at all, since the offerings cancel out
quiz.e: The mishna describes an impure person eating notar of forbidden fat from consecrated food on Yom Kippur — generating sin offerings for chelev, notar, eating sacred food while impure, and eating on Yom Kippur, plus a guilt offering for misusing consecrated property.
